nodes.name: Cork oak
nodes.desc: An evergreen oak of the park's Mediterranean woodland. Red deer and wild boar feed on its acorns and foliage.

nodes.name: Rockrose scrub
nodes.desc: Sage-leaved rockrose, one of many shrubs of the dry scrub, grazed by red deer and other herbivores.

nodes.name: Sea Club-rush
nodes.desc: A sedge of the brackish and freshwater marsh edges that grows where the marisma floods.

nodes.name: Marsh algae & diatoms
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae in the shallow marsh water. Flamingos filter algae and diatoms from the mud and water.

nodes.name: European rabbit
nodes.desc: Grazes grasses and shoots and is the staple food of the Iberian lynx and Spanish imperial eagle. Disease has cut its numbers badly.

nodes.name: Red deer
nodes.desc: Large grazer and browser of the scrub and woodland, and the most recorded mammal in the GBIF data around the park.

nodes.name: Fallow deer
nodes.desc: A smaller deer present in the park. Young fallow deer are sometimes taken by the Iberian lynx.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: A versatile omnivore that digs roots, eats acorns and seeds, and also takes small animals and carrion.

nodes.name: Red swamp crayfish
nodes.desc: A North American crayfish introduced to Spain for cultivation. It spreads easily in disturbed wetlands and now feeds many wading birds and otters.

nodes.name: Eurasian coot
nodes.desc: An abundant marsh bird and a staple of the winter waterfowl crowds, taken by eagles and other predators.

nodes.name: Greater flamingo
nodes.desc: Stirs up shallow mud and filters out small crustaceans, algae, seeds and larvae. Seen in large numbers on the marisma.

nodes.name: Egyptian mongoose
nodes.desc: A common Iberian carnivore that hunts rabbits, birds, reptiles and amphibians. The Iberian lynx often kills it.

nodes.name: Common genet
nodes.desc: A small night-hunting carnivore that takes rodents, rabbits, birds and reptiles. The Iberian lynx often kills genets.

nodes.name: Eurasian otter
nodes.desc: Eats mainly fish, plus amphibians, crustaceans and waterbirds. Here that includes coots and the introduced crayfish.

nodes.name: Grey heron
nodes.desc: A wading bird of the marshes that eats fish, frogs and crayfish. The park holds one of the largest heronries in the Mediterranean.

nodes.name: White stork
nodes.desc: Hunts frogs, reptiles, small mammals and crayfish in marsh and pasture, and is a summer visitor that winters in Africa.

nodes.name: Iberian lynx
nodes.desc: About three-quarters of its food is European rabbit. It also takes ducks, young deer and smaller carnivores such as mongooses and genets.

nodes.name: Spanish imperial eagle
nodes.desc: An endangered eagle that eats rabbits and, where rabbits are scarce, water birds such as coots and ducks.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Hot dry summers set the Mediterranean rhythm of growth in the scrub and woodland.

nodes.name: Autumn-winter rain
nodes.desc: Rainfall drives the flooding of the marshes. Wikipedia notes that very low water in January 2024 gave the lowest bird count on record.

nodes.name: Marisma flooding
nodes.desc: Seasonal flooding of the Guadalquivir delta marshes makes the shallow lagoons that waterbirds and wintering waterfowl depend on.

nodes.name: Sand dunes & soils
nodes.desc: Fixed and mobile dunes and sandy soils carry the pine, scrub and cork oak woodland beside the marsh.

nodes.name: Fungi, dung beetles & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil and marsh mud.
